The curated database

Every substance MuroLens ships with, in one table. This is the same data the Analyse search space and the Resolve candidate lookup are built from, so what is here is what those two are using. Sort by any column, stack the filters, and export whatever survives.

Exports the rows currently shown, in the order shown.

Resolve

isomer discrimination by diagnostic ions
no mass entered

Resolve an observed mass against the database

Give the precursor you observed and the MS/MS peaks that go with it. MuroLens pulls every database structure within tolerance, works out which ions separate them, checks the spectrum for those ions, and ranks the candidates. It reports which ions it found and which it expected but did not, because an absent diagnostic ion is evidence too.

MS/MS peak list

Intensity is optional. The resolver searches the built-in curated database and whatever you have built in the Build section, so build there first if you are testing your own structure. Anything else can be typed below, one PGLang structure per line.

Diagnostic ions between isomers

Isobaric structures (3-3 vs 4-3 cross-links, or a residue that moved position) share a precursor mass but fragment differently. Enter two or more PGLang structures — one per line — and MuroLens lists the ions that belong to only one of them. Those are the peaks worth hunting for in MassLynx.

1 · Runs ▼

Drop .mzML files several at once is fine

Waters .raw folders are a closed binary format and must be converted first — see below.

Converting your .raw ▼

Install ProteoWizard (free, Windows) — it ships with the Waters reader. Open Command Prompt where your .raw folders live and run:

msconvert *.raw --mzML --64 --zlib ^
  --filter "peakPicking vendor msLevel=1-" ^
  -o mzml

peakPicking vendor centroids using Waters' own algorithm. It sharpens the masses and takes a 1 GB run down to roughly 80 MB. Keep both MSE functions in the file — MuroLens quantifies from function 1 and reads fragments from function 2.

Still too big? Add --filter "threshold absolute 100 most-intense".

2 · Search space ▼

Every class you switch on widens the search space and therefore the chance of a coincidental mass match. Leave off anything your organism cannot make.

Gram-negative sacculi are lightly cross-linked, so trimers are usually enough. Gram-positives such as S. aureus run to 80–90% cross-linking and genuinely contain tetramers and higher — but each extra order multiplies the search space, so raise this only when the trimer abundance says there is more to find.

A custom CSV needs Structure and Monoisotopicmass columns, as PGFinder expects. Optional: Stems and Anhydro. Comma-, semicolon- and tab-separated files all work, with either a decimal point or a decimal comma, and names that contain commas can be quoted.

3 · Search settings ▼

These two throw out the one-scan spikes and single-isotope blips that otherwise flood the feature list and soak up random database matches.

Isobars such as a 3-3 and a 4-3 trimer have identical exact masses, so they are always reported together. Raise this to your full tolerance to keep every candidate.

4 · Diagnostic fragment ions ▼

One per line, as label: m/z or just m/z. MuroLens looks for these in the high-energy function at the retention time of whichever peak you select.

What this does

MuroLens turns an LC-MS run of a mutanolysin-digested peptidoglycan sample into a quantified muropeptide profile, in one pass, in your browser.

It replaces the usual MaxQuant → PGFinder → Excel chain. From an mzML file it picks peaks, groups isotopes, assigns charge, back-calculates neutral masses, stitches them into chromatographic peaks, matches them against a muropeptide database, and reports relative abundances along with the cross-linking index and glycan chain length.

Everything runs locally. No file leaves your machine, nothing is uploaded, and it works with the network off — useful on an instrument workstation.

Getting your data in

Waters .raw folders cannot be read directly. The _FUNC00n.DAT files inside them are an undocumented binary format that only MassLynx and Waters' own reader can decode. Convert first with ProteoWizard's msconvert, which is free and ships with the Waters reader on Windows:

msconvert *.raw --mzML --64 --zlib --filter "peakPicking vendor msLevel=1-" -o mzml

The peakPicking vendor filter centroids the spectra using Waters' own algorithm. It both sharpens the masses and takes a 1 GB run down to something like 80 MB. Keep both MSE functions in the output: function 1 is the low-energy channel MuroLens quantifies from, function 2 is the high-energy channel it reads fragments from.

Drop one file or several. Each gets an editable group label — put replicates in the same group and the Compare tab will average them.

The UV / analog channel

A Waters run converted with msconvert often carries the PDA or analog channel as a further acquisition function. If the file has more than two functions, a UV / analog function selector appears under the two MSE pickers, defaulting to the spare one. Its trace is then available from the UV button beside TIC and BPC, drawn in plum and clipped to the same retention window as the ion traces.

If the UV trace comes out empty, the likely reason is that msconvert wrote the analog data as an mzML chromatogram element rather than as spectra, which this reader does not walk.

Results and settings can disagree

Changing a control does not re-run anything. The verdict banner, the summary and the peaks table all describe the run that produced them, not the settings currently on screen. When you change a search setting after a run, a red settings changed since this run notice appears beside the run information; press Identify peaks to bring them back into step.

Note also that Highest oligomer to build limits only the multimer builder. If the reference list you chose contains trimers or tetramers of its own, those remain in the search space.

Choosing a search space

This is the single most consequential choice you make, because the chance of a coincidental match scales with the number of database entries times your mass tolerance. At 15 ppm a 350-entry database matches roughly 0.5% of peaks by accident; a 3000-entry space matches around 5%.

Reference list

  • Gram-negative (mDAP / A1γ) — E. coli, Salmonella, Vibrio, Pseudomonas, Neisseria, Helicobacter, Myxococcus.
  • Gram-positive — twelve architectures, because there is no single Gram-positive stem: S. aureus iso-Gln with Gly1–5 and Gly4Ser bridges, enterococcal D-Asp and D-Asn, pneumococcal Ala-Ala and Ala-Ser, streptococcal Ala2–3, the whole-stem bridge of M. luteus, the mDAP Gram-positives, mycobacterial N-glycolyl MurNAc, and spore-cortex muramic δ-lactam. Bridges are carried in the structure itself, so a matched entry names the bridge composition — shown in its own bridge column.
  • M. xanthus and a mixed bacterial set for organism-specific work.
  • Custom CSV — needs a Structure column and a Monoisotopicmass column, exactly as PGFinder expects. Optional Stems and Anhydro columns let MuroLens compute the cross-linking index and chain length correctly.

Each list comes in three tiers. Core is canonical stems only — start here. Extended adds modifications, lipoprotein remnants and the common D-amino-acid exchanges. Complex opens all twenty amino acids at the terminal stem positions and is only sensible with sub-5 ppm accuracy and MS/MS confirmation. Each tier contains the one above it.

Picking the architecture

When a Gram-positive list is selected, an organism menu appears. Use it. Searching all twelve architectures at once is the single biggest source of coincidental matches in Gram-positive work, because different organisms' bridges collide in mass:

  • A diglycine bridge and a D-Asn bridge are both 114.043 Da — S. aureus against E. faecium, indistinguishable.
  • A D-Asp bridge on Lys and an amidated mDAP tetrapeptide are both 940.424 Da — Enterococcus against Bacillus.
  • A two-alanine bridge on a tripeptide and a plain pentapeptide stem are the same mass, since the bridge residues and the stem residues weigh the same wherever they sit.

Across the whole Gram-positive complex tier there are 38 such collisions. Narrowing to S. aureus, C. difficile, B. subtilis or E. faecium leaves none. If you know your organism, this one menu is worth more than any tolerance setting.

MuroLens reports bridge composition, not sequence. Gly4Ser and Gly3SerGly weigh exactly the same, so permutations are stored once and the residue order is left open. Fixing the order needs MS/MS, or prior knowledge of the strain.

Classes of structure

Switch on only what your organism can actually make. Glycosidic chains, Braun's lipoprotein, Lipid II precursors, recycling products (anhydro-MurNAc peptides such as m(Anh)-AEJA, released by lytic transglycosylases and amidases) and S. aureus-specific species are all off by default, because leaving them on in the wrong organism is a reliable way to manufacture false positives.

Other search-space controls

SettingDefaultWhat it does
Sample was NaBH4-reducedonAll database masses are stored on a reduced basis (MurNAc-ol), which is what a standard digest gives you. Unticking subtracts 2.0157 Da per free reducing end — twice for a cross-linked dimer, not at all for an anhydro species. Getting this wrong shifts everything by 2 Da and you will match nothing.
ModificationsanhydroThirteen monoisotopic deltas that can be applied to every structure. Each one you enable roughly doubles the search space, so add them deliberately. Chemically impossible combinations are blocked automatically — no anhydro on an already-anhydro structure, no modifications on precursors.
Modifications per structureoneAllow one modification at a time, or combinations of two. Two multiplies the space again.
Build cross-linked multimersonA two-stage search: find the monomers first, then assemble dimers and trimers from the ones actually observed, each cross-link costing one H2O. This is how PGFinder expands its space, and it finds cross-linked species your reference list never contained.
Monomer donors12How many of the most abundant observed monomers may seed multimers. Raising it grows the space combinatorially.
Highest oligomerup to trimersGram-negative sacculi are lightly cross-linked and rarely need more. Gram-positives such as S. aureus reach 80–90% cross-linking and genuinely contain tetramers and above, so raise this when the trimer abundance says there is more to find. Each order multiplies the space.
Cross-link chemistry rulesonOnly lets through stem pairs a transpeptidase could actually produce, and labels each with the linkage it implies. See below.

How the cross-link rules work

A 4-3 link is made by a D,D-transpeptidase joining the donor's D-Ala(4) to the acceptor's mDAP(3), or to the N-terminus of the acceptor's bridge. The donor keeps four residues.

A 3-3 link is made by an L,D-transpeptidase joining mDAP(3) to mDAP(3). The donor loses its D-Ala(4), so in the product that stem is a tripeptide.

Two useful consequences follow. A 3-3 product must contain a tripeptide stem, and a 4-3 product must contain a tetrapeptide stem, so many combinations are pinned down outright — two tetrapeptides can only be 4-3, two tripeptides can only be 3-3. Others cannot arise at all: two pentapeptides have no possible donor between them, and a bare Lys-Lys pair has no 3-3 route because lysine lacks mDAP's side-chain carboxyl. Those are dropped from the search space rather than scored, which removes a class of false positive that mass alone cannot see.

The catch worth knowing: gm-AEJ~gm-AEJAA (3-3) and gm-AEJA~gm-AEJA (4-3) have the same exact mass, 1864.8048 Da. MuroLens reports both and marks the row as an isobar. Retention time and MS/MS are the only way to choose — which is exactly the case where the Fragments tab earns its keep.

Search settings

SettingDefaultWhat it does
Mass tolerance15 ppmThe window for a match before calibration. On a well-behaved QTOF you can start lower.
Noise floorautoPeaks below this are ignored. Suggested from the median intensity across three windows spread through the run, not just the header — the noise near the void volume is nothing like the noise where muropeptides elute.
Max charge4Highest charge state considered when grouping isotopes. Trimers commonly reach 3+ or 4+.
Min scans per peak4A chromatographic peak must persist this many scans.
RT from / towhole runRestrict the analysis. Useful for cutting the void volume and a late wash peak.
Min isotope peaks2Rejects single-peak blips. This one filter removes a large fraction of noise features.
Min scans at half height3Rejects one-scan spikes that technically span four scans but are not real peaks.
Merge in-source GlcNAc lossesonFolds the glycosidic-loss satellite eluting at the same time back into its parent, so cone-voltage fragmentation is not counted as a separate species. The loss depends on how the GlcNAc is modified — 203.079 plain, 161.069 de-N-acetylated, 219.074 N-glycolyl, 245.090 O-acetylated — and all four are checked.
Merge sodium adductsoffSame idea for +21.982 Da satellites.
Report co-matches within1 ppmWhen several structures fit one mass, how close they must be to all be reported. Set this to your full tolerance to always keep every candidate.

Accuracy settings

These are the difference between a list of masses within a window and a list of identifications you can defend.

SettingDefaultWhat it does
Recalibrate massesonSearches once wide, finds unambiguous hits with sound isotope envelopes, fits the systematic drift against m/z and retention time, corrects every peak, then searches again tight. Lockspray drift is the usual reason a Waters run sits at 8 ppm instead of 2. On test data with injected drift this cut the RMS error from 6.6 to 0.2 ppm.
Tolerance after calibration6 ppmThe tightened window used for the second pass.
Min anchors5Calibration is skipped below this. The model order also adapts: a constant offset (the median error of the anchors) below twelve, adding the mass term at twelve, the retention-time term at thirty. Overfitting a drift model on ten points does more harm than leaving it alone, but a constant offset on five is safe, and a run with only a few muropeptides needs it as much as any.
Split co-eluting peaksonA 3-3 and a 4-3 dimer are isobaric but separate on the column. Without this they collapse into one entry. The extracted ion trace is cut at genuine valleys so each becomes its own peak.
Valley depth0.55How deep the dip between two maxima must be, as a fraction of the smaller peak, before they are treated as separate. Lower is stricter.
Filter by decoy-calibrated FDRonEvery match is scored on mass error, isotope fit, charge agreement and MS/MS support. A decoy database — the same structures shifted by a whole-dalton ±7 and ±13 Da, which keeps the mass defect real molecules have — is scored identically, and the cutoff is set where the decoy says the error rate crosses your target.
Target FDR1%The false-discovery rate you are willing to accept.
Confirm with MS/MSoffOne extra pass over the high-energy function. Counts the predicted fragment ions of each identification that are present, against what the same ions shifted by ±7 and ±13 Da find by chance, and on every isobar row runs the Resolve engine to pick between the alternatives. Slower, but it is the only thing here that distinguishes isomers.

Diagnostic ions

The Diagnostic fragment ions box takes one ion per line, as label: m/z or just a number. When you select a peak and open the Fragments tab, MuroLens sums every high-energy scan within the retention-time window of that peak and checks your list against the result.

The list is not universal — it follows the reference list you picked. An mDAP organism needs the AEJ / AEJA stem series; a Lys organism such as S. aureus needs AQK stems plus the bridge ladder; C. difficile needs a shifted oxonium because its GlcNAc is deacetylated. Change the reference list or the organism and the box reloads with the right preset. Edit it and your ions are kept and used exactly as written, with a note reminding you they are yours rather than the preset.

With generic markers ticked it also adds the HexNAc oxonium series, and for the selected peak its [M+H]+, the peak left after each GlcNAc neutral loss with its oxonium counterpart, the free peptide stem, and the bridge ladder when the structure has a bridge. The automated Confirm every identification with MS/MS pass is architecture-aware on its own: it reads the stem and bridge out of each matched structure, so it adapts without you doing anything.

203.0794 and 204.0866 are different things

203.0794 Da is the mass of a GlcNAc residue. It is a neutral loss — a gap between two peaks, not a peak. You see it as a precursor losing its GlcNAc.

204.0866 m/z is the HexNAc oxonium ion. It is a charged fragment, a peak you can point at, and it is the one that dominates the low-mass end of a high-energy muropeptide spectrum. It is the residue plus a proton, which is why the two numbers sit one mass unit apart.

Its water losses at 186.0761 and 168.0655 usually appear alongside it. In C. difficile and Listeria, where GlcNAc is largely de-N-acetylated, the oxonium moves down to 162.0761.

What the MS/MS column counts

The MS/MS column — for example 9 vs 0.8 — is the number of predicted fragment ions of the matched structure found in the summed high-energy scans (9), next to the number the same ions shifted by ±7 and ±13 Da find in the same scans (0.8, the average of the four shifts). The prediction comes from the residue graph: B/Y glycan cleavages, b/y stem ions, lactyl-peptide ions, the bridge ladder when there is one, and their neutral losses; the precursor itself is left out because MS1 already measured it. A whole-dalton shift keeps the decoy ions on the mass-defect band real fragments sit on, so the shifted count is what a spectrum this busy hands out by chance. A peak counts as supported when at least three ions are found and the Poisson probability of reaching that count by chance is below 0.01; hover the cell for the numbers.

On an isobar row the question is different — which alternative is it — and the Resolve engine answers it, on the same summed spectrum the Resolve hand-off would send: each alternative's unique ions, tested against its rivals' neutral losses and complementary ions. The pill next to the count says what it concluded: call, lean (provisional), mixture or unresolved; hover it for each candidate's unique ions. The favoured structure moves to the front of the row, and only a call sets the link column, marked ms. The per-candidate ions are in the MS-MS fragments sheet with the role diagnostic.

The Fragments tab shows that predicted set plus your own diagnostic ions and the generic markers, in three labelled blocks. Only the first block feeds the score; the other two are there to look at. Ions appearing in more than one block are listed once, with a small +n badge showing how many other lists also named them.

Found, weak, and not found

A filled dot means the ion was there and cleared 0.2% of the base peak. A hollow dot means a peak sat inside the match window but was too weak to count — at a 50 mDa window the low-mass region of a summed high-energy spectrum nearly always has something in it, so a bare hit is not evidence. Only filled dots are labelled on the spectrum.

If the low-mass ions are all off by the same amount

Waters lockspray anchors the calibration near the reference mass, and below it the fit extrapolates. It is common to see every ion under about 300 Da sitting 10–15 mDa low while ions above 500 Da are within 2 mDa. MuroLens detects that pattern and says so above the table. It means the reported m/z is off down there, not that the assignments are wrong — the ions are real, and their relative intensities are still usable.

MSE fragments everything eluting at once, with no precursor isolation. A fragment found at the right retention time is consistent with your peak, not proof it came from it. If something co-elutes, the ion could be its.

Nomenclature

Every structure name in the table is a compact description of a real molecule. Read it left to right: glycan, then peptide stem, then bridge, then how many stems are joined.

The glycan part

You seeIt means
gmGlcNAc-MurNAc, the disaccharide unit. In a reduced sample the MurNAc is a MurNAc-ol, which is where the +2.0157 Da from NaBH4 sits.
anhgmGlcNAc-1,6-anhydroMurNAc. The terminal unit of a glycan chain. It has no free reducing end, so it is never reduced — which is why counting anhydro units gives you the chain length.
gm-gm-gmA glycan strand with no peptide, released by an amidase. One reducing end per strand, so one reduction whatever the length.
g(-Ac)mThe GlcNAc is de-N-acetylated. Common in C. difficile and Listeria, where it confers lysozyme resistance.
gm(Ac)The MurNAc carries an O-acetyl group at C-6. Common in Neisseria, Pseudomonas, Helicobacter, Staphylococcus.
gm(Glyc)N-glycolyl MurNAc instead of N-acetyl. Mycobacteria, Corynebacterium, Nocardia.
gm(Lactam)Muramic δ-lactam. The marker of spore cortex in Bacillus and Clostridium.
gm(X)M. xanthus modification X, +100.016 Da on the MurNAc.

The peptide stem

Written as one-letter amino-acid codes, in order from position 1. Two of them are not the standard protein codes:

CodeResidue
Jmeso-diaminopimelate (mDAP). Position 3 in most Gram-negatives and in the mDAP Gram-positives. It is the residue that accepts a cross-link and the one that makes 3-3 linkage possible.
Oornithine, in the few organisms that use it at position 3.
KL-lysine at position 3, the Gram-positive alternative to mDAP. Its side-chain amine carries the interpeptide bridge.
QAt position 2 this is iso-glutamine, the amidated form of iso-Glu, standard in S. aureus and the streptococci.
EAt position 2 this is D-iso-glutamate, standard in Gram-negatives.
AAlanine. Position 1 is L-Ala; positions 4 and 5 are D-Ala.

So the two commonest stems you will meet are:

StemReading
AEJAL-Ala – D-iGlu – mDAP – D-Ala. The canonical Gram-negative tetrapeptide.
AEJAAThe same plus a second D-Ala: the pentapeptide, the un-processed form.
AEJThe tripeptide, left behind when a D,D-carboxypeptidase or an L,D-transpeptidase removes D-Ala(4).
AQKAAThe S. aureus pentapeptide: L-Ala – D-iGln – L-Lys – D-Ala – D-Ala.

Bridges and modifications

You seeIt means
[GGGGG]A pentaglycine interpeptide bridge on the Lys side chain — S. aureus. Square brackets always mean a bridge.
[D] / [N]A single D-Asp or D-Asn bridge — E. faecalis and E. faecium respectively.
[AA] / [AS]Ala-Ala or Ala-Ser bridge — S. pneumoniae.
(NH2)The stem is amidated, usually on mDAP or on iso-Glu.
-Lpp(RK)The C-terminal remnant of Braun's lipoprotein, still attached to mDAP. RK in E. coli, TK in Vibrio, YTK in Photobacterium.

The suffix and the joins

You seeIt means
|0Glycan only, no peptide stem.
|1A monomer: one stem.
|2, |3Two or three stems joined. This is the number MuroLens uses for the cross-linking index.
=A cross-link between two stems. gm-AEJA=gm-AEJA (4-3) is a tetra-tetra dimer. The descriptor in brackets says which positions are joined.
~A glycosidic bond: two disaccharide units in one uncleaved strand. gm-AEJA~gm-AEJA is a chain, and it is 2.0157 Da lighter than the cross-linked dimer above, because a chain has one free reducing end and a cross-linked pair has two.
|A vertical bar between two whole names separates alternative structures with the same exact mass. The row is an isobar and MuroLens is not choosing between them.
@RT 9.63Appended when the same structure elutes at more than one resolved retention time, so the rows are separated isomers.

Worked examples

NameWhat it is
gm-AEJA|1Reduced disaccharide-tetrapeptide monomer. The commonest muropeptide in most Gram-negatives, 941.4077 Da.
anhgm-AEJA|1The same but with an anhydro terminus, so it sits at the end of a glycan chain. 921.3815 Da.
gm-AEJA|1~gm-AEJA|1Two tetrapeptides cross-linked. Both stems are tetrapeptides, so this can only be a 4-3 link. 1864.8048 Da.
gm-AEJ|1~gm-AEJAA|1Tripeptide joined to pentapeptide. Because a tripeptide is present, this can only be a 3-3 link — and it has exactly the same mass as the row above.
gm-AQKAA[GGGGG]|1S. aureus pentapeptide monomer carrying its pentaglycine bridge.
g(-Ac)m-AEJA|1C. difficile tetrapeptide with de-N-acetylated GlcNAc.

The notation follows PGFinder, so anything you export can be read straight back into a PGFinder workflow, and any PGFinder database can be loaded here as a custom CSV.

Reading the table

ColumnMeaning
structureThe matched structure in PGFinder compact notation. gm is GlcNAc-MurNAc-ol, anhgm the 1,6-anhydro form, letters are the stem in one-letter code with J for meso-diaminopimelate, square brackets an interpeptide bridge, and the trailing |1 or |2 the oligomerisation state.
scoreComposite of mass error, isotope fit, charge agreement and MS/MS support. Higher is better; it is the ranking that matters, not the absolute number.
q-valueThe false-discovery rate you would accept by keeping this row and everything above it. Below 0.01 is the usual bar.
obs / theo massObserved neutral mass, after calibration, against the database value.
ΔppmThe gap between them. After calibration these should cluster tightly around zero; a spread filling the whole window means coincidence.
isotope fitAgreement between the measured isotope envelope and the one predicted from the candidate's formula, 0 to 1. Above 0.8 is good. A low value with a small Δppm usually means the right mass but the wrong formula.
MS/MSPredicted fragment ions found, against the count the same ions shifted by ±7/±13 Da find by chance; on isobar rows, the Resolve engine's verdict. Only populated if the confirmation pass was run. The individual ions, with observed m/z and mass error, are in the MS-MS fragments sheet of the Excel export and in the saved report.
bridgeThe interpeptide bridge composition, for Gram-positive architectures that have one. Composition only — the residue order is not determined by mass.
link4-3 or 3-3 when every structure that fits the mass has that linkage, or when the MS/MS confirmation made a call (marked ms). A dash means isomers with both linkages fit the mass and nothing decided between them.
RT / widthApex retention time and peak width at half height.
zCharge states the species was seen at, most abundant first. Seeing two or three is a good sign.
area / %Integrated extracted-ion area, and its share of all assigned area.

The tags

  • isobar — several structures share this exact mass. Retention time and MS/MS are the only way to choose between them; the app will not guess.
  • below FDR — the peak matched a structure but scored below the cutoff the decoy search set. These rows are hidden unless Status in Filters includes them; the grey line under the name gives the score and the cutoff.
  • isomer 1/2 — this exact mass elutes at two resolved retention times, so it has been split into separate rows and quantified separately. This is what a 3-3 versus a 4-3 cross-link looks like.
  • split 2 — one of two co-eluting peaks separated out of a single extracted ion trace.
  • dimer / trimer / mod — generated by MuroLens rather than looked up in the reference list.
  • 2×RT — the same structure was found at more than one retention time within one cluster.
  • no match — a detected peak with nothing in the database. Tick show unidentified to see them; they are the honest measure of what you are missing.

Click any row to overlay its extracted ion chromatogram on the trace above. Click a column heading to sort. The chart itself takes a drag to zoom and a double-click to reset.

The verdict banner stays in permanent view above the table, because a result that should not be trusted has to announce itself whatever you are looking at. Clicking it opens the Summary tab.

The metric tiles have moved into that Summary tab so the peak list gets the screen, and the tab carries considerably more than the old strip did: cross-linking broken down by linkage, composition, mass accuracy with the fitted drift model, confidence including the decoy and MS/MS figures, and the peak-detection counts through each filtering stage — each row with a line saying what it means.

Hide chart collapses the chromatogram when you want the table full-height.

The Compact button trims the table to what identifies a peak — structure, score, mass, Δppm, linkage, bridge, retention time and abundance — and hides the diagnostic columns. Switch it off when you want the isotope fit, MS/MS counts, peak width and charge states as well. The metrics above the table are split into two bands: profile, which is what the sacculus is made of, and quality, which is how much you should trust it.

The quality panel

The banner above the metrics gives a plain verdict on whether the table means anything. Four numbers drive it:

  • 3-3 and 4-3 cross-links — the cross-linking index split by linkage, plus an undetermined share. M. xanthus and C. difficile are enriched in 3-3; most Gram-negatives are predominantly 4-3. If the undetermined share is larger than the determined one, treat the split as partial.
  • Assigned ion current — the share of detected signal that got an identification. Below 20% means most of what eluted is not in your search space, or the sample is not mostly peptidoglycan.
  • Decoy false matches — how many peaks an impossible database matched, relative to your real ones. Above about 30% and the table is largely coincidence.
  • Δppm mean ± sd — genuine identifications cluster tightly. A spread filling half the tolerance window is the signature of random matching.
  • Mass calibration — RMS error before and after. A large improvement means drift was found and removed; "not applied" means there were too few anchors.

The Δppm chart view plots mass error against neutral mass with bubble size as abundance. A sloping or curved cloud means calibration drift; a flat scatter across the whole window means coincidence.

Cross-linking index and glycan chain length are computed on the muropeptide subset only, excluding precursors and glycosidic chains, and from MS intensity. Glauner's original definitions use UV peak areas, and MS response varies between species. Treat these as relative profiles rather than a drop-in replacement for UV quantification.

Comparing samples

Load several mzML files at once, give each a group label, and run once. The Compare samples tab gives a structure-by-sample abundance matrix, per-group mean and standard deviation, and a log2 fold change when there are exactly two groups, plus a cross-linking index and chain length row per run. That is the entire replicate-consolidation step from the PGFinder protocol.

Getting the results out

Export Excel writes a real .xlsx across three sheets:

  • Summary — every search setting, then per run the composition, the cross-linking split, and the full quality block including the fitted calibration model. With several runs loaded it also carries the abundance comparison matrix.
  • Identified peaks — one row per structure, with sample and group columns so several runs sit in one table.
  • Unidentified peaks — what was detected but not matched, largest first, with each peak's share of the run and why it was not assigned.
  • MS-MS fragments — one row for every predicted fragment ion of every identified peak, whether or not it was found (role support), plus, on isobar rows, each alternative's unique ions (role diagnostic). This is the sheet behind the MS/MS column: where that column says 9, this sheet lists the predicted ions and which nine of them were there.

The MS-MS fragments sheet

ColumnMeaning
StructureThe identified peak the ions were predicted for.
Candidate, RoleWhich structure's prediction the ion comes from. support rows are the matched structure's predicted ions; diagnostic rows are the ions only that candidate makes among the row's alternatives, which is what the isobar verdict rests on.
PrecursorNeutralMass, PrecursorRT_minThe peak itself, so you can tie a row back to the table.
IonLabel, IonTypeWhat the ion is: precursor, loss, sugar for the HexNAc series, b for the stem ladder, y for glycan+stem ions, stem for the free peptide, bridge for interpeptide bridge ions.
PredictedMzWhere the ion should be, computed from the structure.
Foundyes or no, judged against the detection floor in the last column.
ObservedMz, Delta_mDaWhere it actually was, intensity-weighted across the summed scans, and by how much it missed. A found ion sitting tens of mDa off is worth a second look.
SummedIntensity, RelIntensity_pctAbsolute and relative to the strongest predicted ion for that peak.
ScansSeen / ScansSearchedHow many of the summed high-energy scans the ion appeared in. An ion seen in 2 of 31 scans is weaker evidence than one seen in all 31, even at the same total intensity.
DetectionFloorThe intensity a summed ion had to clear to count as found. It is the larger of the noise floor scaled by scan count and 0.2% of the summed base peak.

Sorting this sheet by Structure then RelIntensity_pct is the quickest way to check an isobar: pull the rows for the two candidate structures and look at which architecture-specific ions actually carry intensity.

This replaced the CSV export for a concrete reason: a charge list like 2/1 and a cross-link type like 4-3 are silently converted to dates when a CSV is opened in Excel. In the .xlsx those cells are written as explicit text and survive intact, while masses and abundances stay numeric with sensible decimal formats.

Save report writes a self-contained HTML file holding the chromatogram as an image, the verdict, the metrics and both tables. A few hundred kilobytes rather than a 200 MB mzML, and it opens in any browser with no analysis and no original data file — useful for sharing a result or looking back at one months later. It is a snapshot, so nothing in it can be re-run; reopen the mzML in MuroLens to change a setting.

A working routine

  1. Convert with the peakPicking filter and keep both MSE functions.
  2. Start with the core tier for your Gram type, ordinary muropeptides only, anhydro as the single modification. Resist widening the space before you have looked at the result.
  3. Run, then read the banner before the table. If calibration ran and the residual is under 2 ppm, your masses are trustworthy.
  4. Check assigned ion current. If it is low, tick show unidentified and look at what the biggest unassigned peaks are — they will tell you whether to widen the search space or whether the sample simply is not mostly peptidoglycan.
  5. Widen one thing at a time: a tier, a class, or a modification. Re-run and watch the decoy rate. If it climbs without the assigned fraction climbing, you have added noise rather than coverage.
  6. For anything tagged isobar or isomer, run the MS/MS confirmation or open the Fragments tab with your own diagnostic ions.
  7. Export the CSV once you are satisfied, and keep it — it records every setting that produced the numbers.

What it cannot do

  • Read Waters .raw directly. Conversion is unavoidable.
  • Resolve isobars on mass alone. Nothing can. Retention time and fragmentation are the only evidence, and both need your judgement.
  • Give absolute quantification. Areas are MS intensities, not molar amounts. Ionisation efficiency differs between species, and no correction factors are applied.
  • Tell you the sample is good. It can tell you a search result is unreliable, which is not the same thing. A clean-looking table from a failed digest is still a failed digest.
  • Substitute for a control. Run a strain you have profiled before, or a standard, and check the app reproduces what you already know before trusting it on something new.

Provenance

Appendix

peptidoglycan rules appendix
—

Every chemical, biological and computational rule MuroLens applies. The constants, residue and modification tables below, and every worked example, are computed by the running engine as you read them rather than typed out, so this appendix cannot drift away from what the app actually does. Where a rule is a modelling choice rather than established chemistry, it says so.

1 · Atomic and physical constants

All masses are monoisotopic. Nothing is stored as a molecular weight; every mass is summed from these constants at run time, so correcting one element propagates everywhere.

The proton, not hydrogen. m/z conversion uses the proton mass. Using the hydrogen atom instead adds 0.000549 Da per charge — 0.6 ppm at m/z 900, inside a 10 ppm window but compounding across charge states.

2 · Building blocks

MurNAc is split into ring and lactyl deliberately. The lactyl is a separate node in the residue graph, which is what makes the L ion series fall out naturally instead of being special-cased.

3 · Amino acid residues

Stored as residue formulas, i.e. the free amino acid minus one water, because the water is added once for the whole molecule.

Stereochemistry is a label, never a mass. D-Ala and L-Ala have the same formula and the same mass. MuroLens carries a stereo field for annotation and retention-time reasoning, but no mass, fragment or score depends on it — because no mass spectrometry can.

4 · Modifications

Every delta is computed from an elemental formula, not typed in as a number.

5 · Reduction

RuleStatement
What is reducibleA sugar that never donates a glycosidic bond, i.e. sits at the reducing terminus of its own chain.
What is notAny sugar that donates a glycosidic bond, and any sugar bearing Anh.
Anhydro blocks it1,6-anhydroMurNAc has its C-1 tied up in the internal bridge, so there is no free reducing end. +2.0157 Da must not be applied.
Glycan chainOne continuous chain has ONE reducing end, so one reduction — not one per unit.
Cross-linked multimerEach unit keeps its own glycan chain, so a dimer has TWO reducing ends and a trimer THREE.
How it is countedPer chain from the graph, never assumed from the oligomer state.

This rule is also how the curated data was corrected. The M. xanthus multimers had been written as glycosidic chains (~), and the anhydro ones then had a reduction subtracted on the strength of their anhydro terminus — which is the right rule for a chain and the wrong one for a cross-linked pair, where the second unit still has a free reducing end. They are cross-links (=) and now carry the published masses, e.g. 1844.7786 Da for TetraTetraAnh. A chain and a cross-linked oligomer of the same composition differ by exactly 2.0157 Da per extra unit, which is the fingerprint to look for: at ~1845 Da that is 1093 ppm, so a 10 ppm search finds one and never the other.

6 · Worked examples, computed now

7 · Bonds and assembly

A structure is a graph of residues joined by typed bonds. Total mass = Σ residues + Σ modifications + one H₂O.

BondWrittenJoinsLoses
glycosidic~sugar → sugar, β-1,4one H₂O
etherimplicitMurNAc ring ↔ its lactyl—
stem-lactyl → residue 1one H₂O
peptideadjacencyresidue n → residue n+1one H₂O
crosslink=donor C-terminus → acceptor side chainone H₂O
branch[ ]lateral chain → its anchor residueone H₂O

Because every bond costs one water and the whole molecule gains one back, the bookkeeping is verifiable: complementary b and y fragments from a single cut must sum to the precursor neutral mass. That invariant is tested and holds.

8 · Cross-links and the donor rule

A descriptor is written donor position – acceptor position.

DescriptorEnzymeBond formedDonor stem must be
4-3D,D-transpeptidase (PBP)D-Ala4 → mDAP3 or Lys3exactly a tetrapeptide
3-3L,D-transpeptidase (Ldt)mDAP3 → mDAP3exactly a tripeptide
1-3L,D-transpeptidaseL-Ala1 → mDAP3exactly one residue
any d-a—residue d → acceptor residue aexactly d residues

A transpeptidase releases whatever lies beyond the linkage: D-Ala5 for a 4-3, D-Ala4 for a 3-3, and everything from D-iGlu2 onwards for a 1-3. So a donor stem always ends exactly at its cross-link position, and a donor still carrying its leaving group cannot exist. The acceptor is unconstrained, because the bond is received by the side-chain amine at position 3.

Enforcing this removes donors that were never chemically possible, which cuts the enumerated space substantially — how much depends on the organism and on which other rules apply.

9 · Bridges and lateral chains

RuleStatement
What it isA peptide hanging off a residue side chain: gm-AQK[GGGGG]AA.
MassAdds Σ residues of the bridge minus one bond water. It does not change the stem backbone length.
Donor eligibilityUnaffected. Donor length is counted along the backbone only, because a bridge is a side chain.
AttachmentA chosen stem position, 3 by default — the Lys ε-amine in Gram-positive PG.
Cross-link geometryThe bridge occupies the acceptor's side-chain amine, so the cross-link cannot also bond there: the donor bonds to the free end of the bridge, putting the bridge inside the linkage rather than hanging off it. Mass is identical either way, but fragmentation is not — cleaving within the bridge gives a stepwise ion series that a dead-end side chain could never produce.
EnumerationEvery stem is generated with and without each bridge, so only the bridges you want need listing.

10 · Fragmentation

Fragments come from cutting bonds in the residue graph and taking the connected pieces. Nothing is pattern-matched from a table of expected ions.

SeriesMeaningConvention
Bglycan cleavage, non-reducing side without the bridging oxygenDomon & Costello
Yglycan cleavage, reducing side with the bridging oxygenDomon & Costello
bstem peptide numbered from the glycan outwards; b1 is the lactyl–Ala amide—
ystem peptide from the free end; y1 is the free stem peptide—
Llactyl-peptide ions — these carry the cross-link informationPGN_MS2
b′, y′the same series on the second stem of a multimerprime notation
RuleStatement
Water assignmentA fragment carries H₂O only when every one of its boundary bonds was on the "to" side; otherwise none. This is what lets cross-link-spanning ions come out at full weight.
Cut depthUp to 3 bonds for monomers and dimers, 2 for trimers and larger, within a 60,000 combination budget.
Charge states1+ always; 2+ when the precursor is 2+ or more and the fragment neutral exceeds 700 Da; 3+ when the precursor is 3+ or more and the neutral exceeds 1400 Da; 4+ when the precursor is 4+ and the neutral exceeds 2100 Da. A fragment never carries more charge than its precursor.
Neutral losses−H₂O, −NH₃, and the Glu and Gln side-chain losses. Optional.
CounterpartsEach ion may be offered with its ±H₂O partner at half weight. Optional.
Above the precursorA fragment must be lighter than the precursor, but it may sit above the precursor m/z: a 1+ fragment of a 2+ precursor does exactly that, and for a dimer those are half of the published diagnostic ions. Neutral masses are compared, not m/z.
Not modelledCross-ring sugar cleavages (A and X ions), because fragments come from cutting bonds rather than rings.

Intensity is a modelling choice, not chemistry. Bond weights are glycosidic 1.00, peptide 1.00, ether 0.85, stem 0.80, branch 0.50, cross-link 0.22; the size term is (fragment mass / precursor mass)α with α = 2.2 − 0.04 × energy, and each extra cut decays the score. Presence or absence of an ion is reliable; predicted height is not. Never use it quantitatively, and never let a low predicted intensity argue against a structure.

11 · What MS can and cannot separate

CaseSame mass?Same fragments?Separable by MS/MS?
3-3 vs 4-3 dimeryesnoYES — L ions differ
Donor/acceptor swappedyespartlysometimes
Stereoisomers (LL vs meso)yesYESNO — ever
D-Ala vs L-AlayesyesNO — ever
Different composition, same massyesnousually

The published E. coli discriminators, checked here as you read:

Exclusive, but only as core ions. The table above compares core fragments. Allow neutral losses and the 4-3 isomer reaches 617.2777 and 746.3203 as well, by ammonia loss, so only 889.3785 is exclusive under every setting. The resolver applies the strict test: an ion counts as diagnostic only when no rival can produce it by any loss, counterpart or charge state, which is why a 4-3 dimer has no exclusive ions against its 3-3 isomer — everything it can make, the 3-3 can make too. There the evidence runs the other way: the absence of the 3-3 markers is what argues for the 4-3, and the resolver says so rather than reporting nothing.

Refusing is a valid answer. When candidates differ only in stereochemistry the resolver reports "cannot be resolved by MS/MS" rather than picking one. They are isomeric, not merely isobaric; chromatography or chiral analysis is the only route.

12 · Database generation

RuleStatement
Donor selectionStem length exactly equal to the cross-link donor position.
Acceptor selectionStem length at or above the acceptor position.
Trimer middle unitMust reach the first acceptor position and end exactly at the second donor position.
Modification placementOnly on sugars that can carry them; Anh only on the reducing MurNAc; ring modifications never on a bare lactyl.
Equivalent link ordersDescriptor tuples that are permutations of one another, such as (4-3,3-3) and (3-3,4-3), select the same stem lengths in swapped positions. Since mass is a sum and these descriptors share an acceptor position, the two classes cover an identical set of masses, so one is collapsed away by default. They remain different molecules and MS/MS can usually separate them.
Which unit carries the bridgeThe bond is received by the free end of the bridge, so in an organism that has bridges every acceptor must carry one, and a unit that only donates must not — its bridge would do no work. A middle unit of a trimer legitimately carries a bridge, because that is how it accepted the previous link. The mass is the same wherever the bridge sits, which is why a breach hides inside an isobar group.
Lateral chain anchorsA bridge must bond to a side-chain group, so it can only sit on Lys, Orn, mDAP, Glu, Asp, Ser, Thr or Tyr. Alanine's side chain is a methyl, so a bridge written on an Ala cannot exist however the mass works out. The builder will not place one there and the predictor warns if you type one.
Cap allocationMax-min fairness: every class small enough for an equal share is built complete; only oversized classes are sampled.
SamplingTaken evenly across the whole class, never the first N.
ReportingA Class × Built table with coverage, so a partial build can never look complete.

Why the cap rule matters. The earlier behaviour truncated a flat list in enumeration order, so asking for "4-3, 3-3" could return a database with zero 3-3 cross-links while reporting 20,000 structures built.

13 · User manual

A walkthrough of the whole app. Each section also has its own Guide button describing that section’s controls in detail; this is the route through them.

Before you start

Open Verify once. Nine checks run automatically against values published by other groups. If any fails, this copy is not computing correctly and nothing it produces should be used. Everything runs in the browser: nothing you load is uploaded, so unpublished data and an offline instrument PC are both fine.

A typical run, end to end

StepWhereWhat you do
1—Convert your Waters .raw to mzML with msconvert. Keep both MSE functions: function 1 is quantified from, function 2 supplies the fragments. The command is in the Analyse sidebar.
2BuildOnly if the shipped reference lists do not describe your organism. Start from a preset, edit it, press Estimate size, then Build database, then Use in Analyse.
3AnalyseDrop the mzML files, set the quantify and fragment functions, choose a reference list, set the tolerance and retention window, press Identify peaks.
4AnalyseRead the quality verdict above the table. Work down the Peaks tab: is Δppm within tolerance, did the isotope pattern match, was it confirmed by MS/MS, were co-matches flagged.
5ResolveFor any peak with co-matches, open its Fragments tab, pull the high-energy spectrum and press Resolve this peak. Read the verdict; if it is Provisional, tick two candidates and press Compare selected.
6AnalyseExport Excel for the workbook, Save report for a standalone HTML record.
7VerifyCopy methods paragraph for your manuscript.

The six sections

SectionWhat it is for
StructureOne molecule at a time: type a structure in PGLang, get its formula, mass, adduct m/z, structure map and every predicted fragment. Also scores a pasted peak list against that one structure.
BuildGenerates a search space from a description of the peptidoglycan you expect, and holds the 620-substance curated database as a browsable table.
AnalyseReads mzML, finds and quantifies peaks, matches them against a reference list and confirms them with MS/MS.
ResolveDecides between structures that share a mass, using only the fragment ions unique to each. Willing to refuse.
VerifyLive reference checks, provenance and a methods paragraph.
AppendixThis document.

Things that catch people out

SymptomCause
Results disagree with the settings on screenChanging a control does not re-run anything. A red notice appears next to the run info when settings have changed since the last run.
No MS/MS confirmation on any peakThe high-energy function is not set, or the conversion dropped it.
"Nothing in the database has this mass" in ResolveThe structure is not in the curated set. Build it first, or paste it into the extra-candidates box.
Resolve says "Possible mixture" on a test spectrumYou pasted a complete predicted fragment list. Untick neutral losses and counterparts, and trim to the strongest 20–40 ions.
Resolve says "cannot be resolved by MS/MS"The candidates are stereoisomers. They are isomeric, not merely isobaric; only chromatography or chiral analysis can separate them.
A build returns far fewer structures than expectedA chemistry rule removed the impossible ones — most often a bridge on a donor-only unit, or a donor still carrying its leaving group.
The UV trace is emptySome msconvert settings write the analog channel as a chromatogram rather than as spectra, which this reader does not walk.

What the tool cannot do

Fragment intensities are heuristic — presence is reliable, height is not. Cross-ring sugar cleavages (A and X ions) are not modelled. Stereochemistry is carried as a label and no mass spectrometry can resolve it. SMILES and InChIKey are not produced. A 4-3 dimer has no fragment its 3-3 isomer cannot also produce, so that call rests on the absence of the 3-3 markers rather than on positive evidence. MuroLens has not been peer reviewed, and as of version 1.1 the resolver has been validated against synthetic peak lists rather than real spectra — treat early calls as hypotheses to confirm.

Credit

Fragmentation rules follow Kwan et al., Chem. Sci. 2024, 15, 1846 (PGN_MS2). PGLang and the reference masses come from PGFinder (Patel et al., eLife 2021; Alamán-Zárate et al., Commun. Chem. 2025, 8:91). MuroLens is an independent implementation, not affiliated with either group.
